hypothesisOutcomes.hypothesis: Run enqueue deduplication, claim/heartbeat/lease ownership, stale-worker completion and memory/Postgres differences (RunStore interface)
hypothesisOutcomes.outcome_detail: src/runs/run-store.ts defines the RunStore interface; src/runs/memory-run-store.ts and src/runs/postgres-run-store.ts are structurally divergent implementations of the same contract, not a thin adapter pair. Dedup: memory uses an in-process Map keyed by dedupKey with a settle() EventEmitter; Postgres uses an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE SET id = runs.id single round-trip (postgres-run-store.ts:194-205). Claim: memory filters+sorts an in-memory array by createdAt (memory-run-store.ts:76-84); Postgres uses a correlated subquery with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED plus a retry_after<=now and a NOT IN (running-or-not-yet-retryable) session exclusion, all inside one UPDATE (postgres-run-store.ts:212-232) -- this is materially different concurrency-safety machinery (row-level locking vs single-threaded JS). Stale-worker completion: memory's reapExpired advances leaseToken/leaseExpiresAt via a fresh randomUUID before calling onRetired, so a zombie's later complete()/fail() call is rejected by token mismatch (memory-run-store.ts:206-211, proven by run-store.test.ts 'reaper does not requeue a run whose lease was renewed mid-sweep' and worker-reaper.test.ts 'reapExpired fences the dead attempt ... zombie heartbeat fails'); Postgres does the equivalent fencing with an UPDATE ... RETURNING id guarded by lease_token=$3 AND lease_expires_at<=$4 (postgres-run-store.ts:369-373) before calling onRetired -- same fence-before-release invariant, different mechanism (JS closure vs conditional UPDATE). Heartbeat/lease ownership: proven directly by process-run.test.ts's LEASE_LOST_CONSECUTIVE cancellation logic (worker.ts:22-55) -- N consecutive definitive lost beats cancel the in-flight turn, a single lost beat does not, and a thrown (transient) heartbeat error never counts toward the streak.

hypothesisOutcomes.hypothesis: Retry/error attempt budgets, reaper/requeue/park behavior, graceful drain, cancellation/withdrawal and task protection across actual callers
hypothesisOutcomes.outcome_detail: Two textually distinct parking mechanisms exist and are covered by disjoint code paths and disjoint tests, a distinction the work order's hypothesis text does not itself separate: (a) ERROR-BUDGET parking -- errorAttempts reaches maxAttempts, reason is the caller's own error text (worker-reaper.test.ts 'a run parks once the ERROR budget is exhausted'); (b) CLAIM-CAP parking -- attempts reaches maxClaims regardless of error budget, reason is a synthesized 'suspected crash loop' string UNLESS a concrete error is present on that same claim, in which case the concrete message wins (memory-run-store.ts:276-279, postgres-run-store.ts:176-179, proven by worker-reaper.test.ts 'with maxClaims set ... PARK the poison pill' and 'a concrete error parks with its own message even when over the claim cap'). Reap-only requeues (no kill, no caller) NEVER spend the error budget even after five repeated reaps (worker-reaper.test.ts 'repeated lease-expiry reaps requeue forever without spending the error budget') -- this is a deliberate adverse-tolerant design, not a bug, but it means an infinitely-crashing worker with no maxClaims cap set will requeue the same run forever with errorAttempts staying at 0, only the claim-cap (if configured) bounds it. Graceful drain: DrainController (src/runs/drain.ts) polls InstanceRegistry.beat() every 10s by default and flips canClaim()=false when a newer build's heartbeat is detected, logging the transition; Worker.stop(drainMs) races the in-flight loop against a timeout and hands back an unfinished run's lease AND its session lease via releaseInFlight() (worker.ts:177-196, proven by worker-reaper.test.ts's 8 drain-focused cases including idempotent/collapsed releaseInFlight and a retry-on-failed-unlock backstop). TaskProtection (ECS-specific) is a best-effort side call whose own failures are swallowed with a de-duplicated console.error, never surfaced to the caller (task-protection.ts:26-32) -- a fail-open design for infrastructure protection signaling.

hypothesisOutcomes.hypothesis: Cross-component lifecycle mismatches, loss/duplication/cleanup failure, missing consumers/tests and adverse paths. Distinguish source-guaranteed, asserted-by-test and unknown behavior; prove neither concurrency nor restart guarantees merely from method names or a happy-path test
hypothesisOutcomes.outcome_detail: The strongest cross-component finding in this lane is that RunStore and SessionStore are bound together by TWO DIFFERENT cross-store handback guarantees, not one shared invariant (corrected in this round-2 rework, F2). REAP PATH: reapExpired MUST advance the dead run's lease token (fencing a zombie's late heartbeat to fail) BEFORE calling the onRetired hook that force-releases the STRANDED SESSION lease, and the run only becomes re-claimable AFTER that hook completes -- proven directly, not inferred from names, by worker-reaper.test.ts's 'reapExpired fences the dead attempt, releases its session lease, and only then requeues' (asserts statusAtRelease==='running' and zombieBeatAtRelease===false measured INSIDE the onRetired callback, before the requeue). This IS a database-enforced, caller-independent guarantee: the fence changes the stored token unconditionally. DRAIN PATH: worker.ts's own drain path (releaseInFlight, worker.ts:177-196) does NOT reimplement the same fencing guarantee -- it calls heartbeat() first, and heartbeat() in BOTH backends (memory-run-store.ts:92-97, postgres-run-store.ts:256-262) checks only `status='running' AND lease_token=$token`, with NO comparison of lease_expires_at to the current time. A true heartbeat result therefore certifies token-and-status match, not that the lease's TTL window is still open, and the drain path's overall safety additionally relies on an assumption that the calling worker process is the same process that legitimately holds the token -- a genuinely weaker, caller-trust-dependent argument than the reap path's fence. What IS shared and test-proven across the drain path specifically: releaseInFlight() is idempotent per run (a second call for the same leaseToken is a no-op), collapses concurrent overlapping calls into exactly one underlying unlock, and RETRIES the session unlock on a subsequent call if the first attempt's forceReleaseLease failed (worker.ts:177-196, proven by worker-reaper.test.ts 'releaseInFlight is once-per-run', 'overlapping releaseInFlight calls collapse into one release', and 'a backstop retry still unlocks the session after the first attempt's unlock failed'). A second cross-component chain runs through run-result-delivery.ts (outside the three target trees, read as a direct non-test consumer per the work order's dependency-read allowance): RunStore.onTerminal fires recordRunFailureEntry against SessionStore (idempotent turn_failure entry, suppressed if the orchestrator or web-drain already recorded one by run-id or delivery-key) AND enqueues a redacted Slack recovery note via DeliveryStore -- proven end-to-end by run-result-delivery.test.ts's wired-store cases. A newly-found third chain (round-2 full read of test/orchestrator.test.ts) shows SessionStore's own lease contention differentiates by holder kind independently of the RunStore-side fence/heartbeat question above: a `"turn"`-held session lease causes an immediate session_busy refusal for a competing caller, while a `"compaction"`-held lease instead makes the competing caller WAIT (governed by turnLeaseWaitMs) rather than refuse -- proven by 'a lease held briefly (compaction's write hold) delays the turn instead of refusing it' and 'a session busy refusal is recorded durably with the holder's remaining lock'. A fourth chain runs through turn-bookkeeping-failures.test.ts (orchestrator-level, SessionStore.appendTape failure boundary): a tape-append failure AFTER a surface post has already happened is deliberately classified NonRetryableTurnError (the effect landed; re-running would double-post) while a tape-append failure BEFORE any effect stays retryable -- this pre/post-effect distinction is a genuine, source-verified concurrency/idempotency guarantee, not assumed from a happy-path test. UNKNOWNS explicitly preserved, not converted to no-value: (a) RunActivityStore's memory MAX_PER_RUN cap has no direct test (see H5); (b) session-store.test.ts's backends array contains only 'memory', so no test in the read evidence directly parameterizes SessionStore's lease/tenure semantics against the Postgres implementation, though the Postgres SQL was itself read and independently verified; (c) the drain path's heartbeat-renewal safety argument is NOT independently proven against an expired-but-unreaped lease scenario in this corpus, and this gap is preserved rather than smoothed into an equivalence claim with the reap path's fence.

mechanismRecords.verifier: This mechanism is FOUR distinct, independently-verified concurrency guards, not one -- the pre-rework record conflated them (F3 finding, round 1). (a) enqueue() idempotency-key dedup: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO UPDATE SET id = runs.id (postgres-run-store.ts:194-205, declarative, no catch needed for a same-key race specifically) -- CORRECTED in round 2: this statement is NOT wrapped in a try/catch in enqueue(), so while a same-idempotency_key race is handled declaratively without throwing, enqueue() does NOT 'never throw' or 'always succeed' in the general case -- any other database-level failure on that same INSERT (connection loss, deadlock, an unrelated constraint violation, a timeout) propagates as a thrown error like any unguarded query, exactly as it would without the ON CONFLICT clause. The ON CONFLICT clause only removes the NEED for a catch on the idempotency-key race specifically; it is not a blanket success guarantee. (b) claim()/claimById() PRIMARY one-per-session defense: the UPDATE's own 'session_id NOT IN (SELECT session_id FROM runs WHERE status='running')' subquery, evaluated inside the same statement as the row selection. (c) claim()/claimById() BACKSTOP: the partial unique index idx_runs_one_running_per_session (line 80) plus an isUniqueViolation() catch (lines 228-231, 250-253) -- this backstop protects the RACE WINDOW of (b), i.e. two concurrent claims both passing the NOT-IN check before either commits; it is UNRELATED to idempotency_key. (d) lease fencing: a fresh leaseToken is issued on every successful claim and required by every subsequent mutation (fail/complete/heartbeat), fencing a zombie's stale token out.

mechanismRecords.userAgentOutcome: A worker holding a run's lease is detected as dead (crashed, network-partitioned, or deploy-drained) within a bounded number of missed heartbeats, and the in-flight turn is cancelled so its result cannot land after the run has already been reassigned.

mechanismRecords.userAgentOutcome: A run that keeps crashing is eventually parked as terminally failed instead of retrying forever, but the operator sees the REAL error message when one is available, not a generic crash-loop label that would hide the actual cause.
mechanismRecords.verifier: Two independent parking triggers exist in the SAME retire()/park function: (a) errorAttempts >= maxAttempts (the caller-supplied error budget), and (b) attempts >= maxClaims (an optional, separately-configured claim-count cap) -- proven as textually distinct by worker-reaper.test.ts's 'a run parks once the ERROR budget (error_attempts) is exhausted' (no maxClaims involved) versus 'with maxClaims set, repeated lease-expiry reaps PARK the poison pill instead of requeuing forever' (errorAttempts stays 0 throughout, only attempts/claim-count triggers the park). When the claim-cap park has NO concrete error (pure reap-triggered), the stored reason is a synthesized 'suspected crash loop' string; when a concrete caller error IS present on the claim-cap-triggering attempt, that real message wins over the synthesized one -- proven by 'a concrete error parks with its own message even when over the claim cap' asserting the reason matches /real boom/ and explicitly does NOT match /crash loop/.
mechanismRecords.nonTestConsumer: src/runs/worker.ts:90-93 (worker.ts's fail() call after a caught turn exception passes the real error through processRun -> runs.fail -> retire, which is where the two-trigger logic applies)
mechanismRecords.integrationLink: Both parking triggers flow through the same terminal write path and both call settle()/emit onTerminal listeners identically, so downstream consumers (e.g. run-result-delivery.ts) cannot distinguish which trigger fired from the terminal event alone -- only from reading the stored result.reason text, which is itself not a structured field (no distinct terminal-reason enum value separates 'error-budget park' from 'claim-cap park' from 'age-cap park' from 'ordinary NonRetryable park' in the Run type; all four produce status:'failed' with only a free-text reason string differing).

mechanismRecords.userAgentOutcome: The model's streamed reply accumulates per run in a bounded buffer that a poller can read at any time; once the run ends, the buffer survives briefly so a final poll can still catch it, then is evicted -- unless a late delta arrives, which cancels the pending eviction and keeps streaming.

mechanismRecords.userAgentOutcome: Two DIFFERENT guarantees protect a run's session write-lock against a zombie holder, not one shared guarantee, and the drain path's guarantee is narrower than an independent safety proof (F2 correction, round 2). REAP PATH: when a worker is detected dead via lease-expiry sweep, its stale lease token is FENCED (replaced with a fresh random token) BEFORE the cross-store session lock is released, so the zombie's eventual late completion attempt is rejected by the fence -- this IS an independent, source-verified proof, because the fence changes the stored token itself. DRAIN PATH: when a worker is asked to gracefully stop mid-turn, it calls heartbeat() first; heartbeat() in BOTH backends checks only `status='running' AND lease_token=$token` (memory-run-store.ts:92-97; postgres-run-store.ts:256-262) -- NEITHER backend's heartbeat compares `lease_expires_at` against the current time. A heartbeat therefore returning true proves only 'this record still says running, still holds this exact token' -- it does NOT independently prove the lease has not already expired past its TTL while a slow reaper sweep has not yet caught up. The drain path's actual safety rests on an assumption outside what heartbeat() itself checks: that the calling worker process is the same process that legitimately holds the token and has not, in fact, stalled. This is a materially weaker basis than the reap path's fence, which changes the token unconditionally and needs no assumption about which process is calling it.

mechanismRecords.verifier: REAP PATH (genuine fence-before-release): worker-reaper.test.ts's 'reapExpired fences the dead attempt, releases its session lease, and only then requeues' asserts, MEASURED INSIDE the onRetired callback itself, that the run's status is still 'running' (not yet requeued) AND that a heartbeat using the zombie's ORIGINAL lease token already fails -- proving the fence (memory-run-store.ts:207) happens strictly before session-lease release, which happens strictly before requeue-availability. This is genuine token fencing: a fresh random token invalidates the zombie's old one, independent of any assumption about caller identity. DRAIN PATH (heartbeat-renewal, weaker than fencing -- confirmed by direct source re-read in round 2): src/runs/worker.ts:177-196's releaseInFlight() calls heartbeat() first. heartbeat()'s SQL/logic in both backends is `WHERE id=$runId AND lease_token=$token AND status='running'` with NO comparison of lease_expires_at to the current time (memory-run-store.ts:92-97; postgres-run-store.ts:256-262, re-verified directly against source in this round-2 rework). A true return therefore certifies only token-and-status match, not that the TTL window is still open. The subsequent forceReleaseLease(session) and releaseLease(run) calls proceed on that certification. Safety in the drain path is NOT purely a property heartbeat() itself proves -- it additionally relies on this being the worker's OWN graceful-stop code path calling it about its OWN still-in-flight run, i.e. an assumption about which process is invoking releaseInFlight(), not a database-enforced guarantee independent of the caller. This is a genuinely different, and weaker, safety argument than the reap path's fence, and the pre-rework record's claim that both paths 'guarantee a session lock is never released while a run-side actor might still be mutating it' OVERSTATED the drain path specifically -- that sentence is withdrawn (see userAgentOutcome above) rather than defended, since no test in this corpus independently proves the drain path safe against an expired-but-unreaped lease scenario. releaseInFlight() is idempotent per run (a second call for the same leaseToken is a no-op, proven by 'releaseInFlight is once-per-run'), collapses concurrent overlapping calls into exactly one underlying unlock (proven by 'overlapping releaseInFlight calls collapse into one release'), and RETRIES the session unlock if the first attempt's forceReleaseLease failed (proven by 'a backstop retry still unlocks the session after the first attempt's unlock failed') -- these three properties ARE test-proven and remain valid regardless of the withdrawn sentence above.
mechanismRecords.nonTestConsumer: This is itself the direct cross-tree (src/runs -> src/sessions) integration point the work order's hypothesis 6 named explicitly; createReaper(runs, sessions, opts) binds both stores' lifecycle together at construction for the reap path; worker.ts's stop()/releaseInFlight() binds them for the drain path. test/web-transcript-delivery.test.ts (found in the F1 rework's corrected discovery) reveals a THIRD, separate lease-interaction pattern outside worker.ts entirely: web delivery writes WAIT for a busy session lease to free before writing ('a busy session lease holds the delivery back, unacked, until the write lands'), and give up LOUDLY (never silently) after a fixed wedge window ('a lease wedged past the giveup window degrades to a loud nudge-only delivery') -- this is neither the reap fence nor the drain heartbeat, but a third, consumer-side lease-aware coordination pattern. test/orchestrator.test.ts's 'session busy' cases (round-2 full-read finding, lines 3206-3338) additionally show that a `"turn"`-held session lease causes an immediate refusal for a competing caller, while a `"compaction"`-held lease instead makes the competing caller WAIT (turnLeaseWaitMs) rather than refuse -- confirming that SessionStore's own lease semantics differentiate by holder kind independently of the RunStore-side fence/heartbeat distinction this record concerns.
mechanismRecords.integrationLink: The reap path (background sweep, fence-then-release, a callback invoked mid-reapExpired) and the drain path (foreground graceful stop, heartbeat-then-release, an explicit async releaseInFlight method) are TWO SEPARATE mechanisms with the SAME OUTCOME ORDERING (session lock released only after a run-side check is performed) but DIFFERENT and NON-EQUIVALENT safety arguments (fencing, which is a database-enforced guarantee independent of caller identity, vs. heartbeat-renewal, which certifies only token-and-status match and additionally relies on caller-identity assumptions) -- a future change to one path would not automatically keep the other consistent, and describing both as 'the same guarantee' (as the original pre-rework record did, and as this record's own round-1 rework still partly implied by using 'never ... still be mutating' language) overstates what the drain path's own test suite and source actually prove.
mechanismRecords.tests: test/worker-reaper.test.ts (8 of 20 cases cover this mechanism): reap-path fence-then-release ('reapExpired fences the dead attempt, releases its session lease, and only then requeues', 'reaping a lease-expired run releases its stranded session lease', 'a heartbeat landing between SELECT and retire leaves the run AND its session lease untouched'); drain-path heartbeat-then-release ('draining a worker mid-turn hands back the session write-lock, not just the run lease', 'releaseInFlight is once-per-run', 'overlapping releaseInFlight calls collapse into one release (graceful stop vs backstop)', 'a backstop retry still unlocks the session after the first attempt's unlock failed', plus the thrown-claim/stop-budget cases). test/web-transcript-delivery.test.ts (NEW): the third lease-wait/giveup pattern cited above.
mechanismRecords.failureSemantics: REAP PATH: if the session-lease release itself fails (simulated as a thrown forceReleaseLease inside onRetired), the run is deliberately kept in 'running' status rather than handed back prematurely -- a fail-safe (not fail-open) design. DRAIN PATH: releaseInFlight() retries the session unlock on a subsequent call if the first attempt failed (the 'backstop retry' test simulates one transient failure then a successful retry); if heartbeat() itself returns false (token or status mismatch -- e.g. because a reaper already fenced this run in the interim), releaseInFlight does not proceed to release anything. heartbeat() returning true does NOT distinguish 'genuinely still within TTL' from 'record unclaimed by anyone else yet, TTL possibly already lapsed' -- both backends' heartbeat query has no lease_expires_at comparison, so this distinction is architecturally unavailable to the drain path, not merely untested.
mechanismRecords.sourceNativeStatus: QM wires and uses this natively across both the background reaper and the foreground worker drain path.
mechanismRecords.cvfComparisonOwner: OWNER_NOT_FOUND. This is a composite of M3 (no CVF reaper) and M6 (no CVF tenure/holder-kind session lease) -- since neither half of either cross-store invariant (reap-fence-then-release, or drain-heartbeat-then-release) has a CVF owner independently, neither composite has an owner to compare against.
mechanismRecords.deltaBeyondCvf: Two independently-implemented, differently-reasoned cross-store handback orderings (reap: fence, then release, then reclaim -- a strong, caller-independent guarantee; drain: renew-if-still-matching-token, then release -- a weaker guarantee that additionally assumes correct caller identity) both aiming to avoid releasing a session lock while a run-side actor might still be mutating it, but only the REAP path actually proves that outcome independently of caller trust. This asymmetry -- not a single unified guarantee -- is the genuinely reusable design lesson for any future CVF multi-store work-queue-plus-session-lock architecture: a graceful-drain handback path should either add its own TTL check to heartbeat-equivalent calls, or be explicitly documented as trusting caller identity rather than providing a database-enforced proof, so a future implementer does not assume it is as strong as the reap-side fence.
mechanismRecords.practicalBenefit: No CVF surface currently combines a durable work queue and a durable session/conversation lock, so there is nothing to enrich today. Recorded as the strongest design-reference finding in this audit for if/when such an architecture is proposed: it should adopt the reap path's fence-before-release pattern as the model for involuntary-loss handling, but should NOT assume the drain path's heartbeat-renewal pattern provides an equivalent independent safety guarantee -- either add a TTL check to any heartbeat-equivalent used for voluntary handback, or explicitly document that path as trusting the calling worker's own liveness rather than proving it, which is the exact distinction this rework (F2, round 2) corrected after round 1 still implied equivalence.
mechanismRecords.nextActionTrigger: Reopen if CVF proposes any architecture combining a durable work queue with a durable session/conversation lock. Both orderings should be explicit, separately-reasoned design requirements from day one: fence-before-release for involuntary loss (a strong, caller-independent guarantee to copy directly), and EITHER a TTL-aware heartbeat-equivalent OR an explicit caller-identity-trust documentation for voluntary handback (QM's own drain path does neither, which any adopting design should improve on rather than copy verbatim).

mechanismRecords.userAgentOutcome: A failure that happens AFTER an observable side-effect has already occurred (e.g. a message was already posted to the user) is never silently retried, which would double the effect; a failure BEFORE any effect occurred is retried normally, since nothing externally visible happened yet.

mechanismRecords.verifier: test/turn-bookkeeping-failures.test.ts directly proves the boundary by INJECTING a failure at exactly the turn-end coverage-append call, AFTER a mid-turn surface post has already succeeded: the resulting rejection IS a NonRetryableTurnError with message matching /coverage append failed/, the surface post is confirmed to have landed exactly once (posted===['ok']), and the session's tape-coverage watermark is deliberately left BELOW the latest entry seq so a future heal pass can cover the gap rather than the worker blindly re-executing the whole turn. The paired case injects the SAME KIND of failure (an appendTape throw) but at a PRE-EFFECT point (before any surface post) and proves the resulting error is explicitly NOT a NonRetryableTurnError, i.e. the retry path stays open -- same failure mechanism (appendTape throwing), opposite retryability classification, purely based on WHEN in the turn it occurs relative to an observable side-effect.

Bounded search found EXTENSIONS/CVF_MODEL_GATEWAY/src/fallback-policy.ts (FallbackPolicy.decide) as the nearest adjacent CVF surface -- it classifies retryable_or_unknown_failure vs non_retryable_status PURELY from HTTP status-code membership in a static list ([408,409,429,500,502,503,504]) plus a maxAttempts cap; it has NO concept of whether an observable side-effect already occurred before the failure -- its classification axis (status code) is orthogonal to QM's (effect-occurred vs not).
mechanismRecords.deltaBeyondCvf: The side-effect-aware (not status-code-aware) retryability classification is a materially different and more sophisticated axis than CVF's existing narrower classifier; adopting it would require CVF's own retry logic to track 'has an externally-visible effect happened yet' as first-class state, which FallbackPolicy's current single-call LLM-provider-fallback scope does not need (a provider call is either atomic-and-failed or atomic-and-succeeded from FallbackPolicy's vantage point; it never spans an intermediate already-posted-a-message state).
mechanismRecords.practicalBenefit: The side-effect-aware retry classification (never retry past an observable effect; always retry before one) is a sharper, more specific requirement than CVF's existing FallbackPolicy retryable/non-retryable HTTP-status classification (EXTENSIONS/CVF_MODEL_GATEWAY/src/fallback-policy.ts), which has no side-effect-occurred awareness at all today. If CVF's model gateway or any future durable-run surface ever needs to retry a multi-step operation that can partially complete (post a message, then fail before recording success), this distinction is the missing piece FallbackPolicy would need to add, and QM's tests already demonstrate the exact boundary condition (a failure landing exactly at the side-effect boundary) that any adopting implementation must get right.
mechanismRecords.nextActionTrigger: Reopen if CVF's execution plane grows multi-step workflows where an intermediate step can have an observable, non-idempotent side effect before the overall unit of work completes or fails.

findings.F2_round2: M13's userAgentOutcome/deltaBeyondCvf/practicalBenefit still asserted, in substance, that both the reap and drain paths independently guarantee a session lock is never released while a run-side actor might still be mutating it. Direct re-read of memory-run-store.ts:92-97 and postgres-run-store.ts:256-262 confirms heartbeat() in BOTH backends checks only status and lease_token equality, with NO comparison of lease_expires_at against the current time -- so a true heartbeat does not, by itself, prove the lease has not already expired past its TTL while an unrelated slow reaper sweep has not yet caught up. The drain path's actual safety additionally depends on an assumption about caller identity (the worker calling releaseInFlight is presumed to be the same process that legitimately holds the token), which is not something heartbeat() itself verifies. The over-strong claim is withdrawn from M13's userAgentOutcome and replaced with an explicit statement of what IS and is NOT independently proven for each path; H6's outcome_detail is resynced to match, since it still described the drain path using 'independently reimplements the SAME run-lease-then-session-lease handback order' language that implied fencing-equivalent strength.
findings.F3_round2: M1's tests field described test/postgres-store.test.ts:1523 as asserting that the 'LOSING attempts' errors' from 8 concurrent claim() calls match /idx_runs_one_running_per_session/ -- this is not what the test does. Direct re-read confirms the regex-matched error assertion is against a RAW `UPDATE runs SET status='running'` issued directly via pg.Pool (bypassing claim() entirely) against an already-running session; the 8 concurrent claim() calls in the SAME test only assert `raceClaims.length === 0` (no double-claim), with claim() itself returning null for losers, not throwing or producing a caught error. M1's tests field is corrected to describe the actual three-part assertion structure (raw-UPDATE rejection proves the unique-index backstop; claimById returning null proves the primary NOT-IN exclusion; 8-way concurrent claim() proves the end-to-end no-double-run outcome without asserting per-loser errors). Separately, M1's verifier and failureSemantics fields both claimed enqueue()'s ON CONFLICT clause means it 'never throws' or 'always succeeds' -- corrected to state precisely that ON CONFLICT handles a same-idempotency_key race declaratively without a catch, but enqueue()'s INSERT is not wrapped in any try/catch, so any other database-level failure (connection loss, deadlock, an unrelated constraint violation) still propagates as a thrown error exactly as an unguarded INSERT would.
findings.F5_round2: M10's integrationLink field still read 'N/A within target-tree scope ... not re-read here', directly contradicting its own nonTestConsumer field two lines above, which already carried the concrete wiring.ts/orchestrator.ts trace from the round-1 rework -- the round-1 edit to nonTestConsumer was never propagated to integrationLink.
